The Medieval Wars, c.1180–1500

Eight battles from the storm of a crusader castle in 1179 to the Swiss at Dornach in 1499: a siege and a raid in the Latin East, the longbow battles of the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of the Roses, Portugal against Castile, the Danes at the gate of Visby, and the Confederates against the Landsknechte. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the medieval armies' figures, the wound tables their battles roll on, and the battlefields.

The battlefields: Jacob's Ford 1179, Sidon 1253, Crécy 1346, Visby 1361, Aljubarrota 1385, Agincourt 1415, Towton 1461, Dornach 1499.

The period's fighting

The battles in this book run from 1179 to 1499. Most of what armies did in those years was not battle at all. It was marching, raiding, besieging and waiting.

Armies

Until the very end of the period, men were raised for a campaign and sent home after it. A great lord brought his retinue: his household knights, squires and servants, and the men who held land from him. In England from the 1340s most of this was done by indenture, a written contract. A captain agreed to bring so many men-at-arms and so many archers, for so long, at set daily wages. In 1415 most contracts asked for three archers to every man-at-arms.

Below the retinues were the levies: townsmen and peasants called out to defend their own country. They were the Gotlanders at Visby and the Swiss cantons' men. Beside them served mercenaries, hired by the company: Genoese crossbowmen in French pay, English archers in Portugal, and by 1499 the German Landsknechte. In the Latin East and the Baltic the military orders kept the nearest thing to a professional army. Templars, Hospitallers and Teutonic Knights were monks under vows who fought for life.

Arms and armour

In 1180 a knight wore mail, a shirt of riveted iron rings, over a padded coat. Mail turned a cut well and a thrust less well. Through the 1300s plates were added: first at the knees and elbows, then a breastplate under cloth. By about 1420 a rich man-at-arms wore a full harness of plate and needed no shield. A poorer man wore a jack, a coat of many layers of linen, and an iron hat.

The missile weapons changed the battle. The crossbow was powerful and easy to learn, but slow. The English longbow shot perhaps 10 arrows a minute, and in massed bands it broke French charges at Crécy and Agincourt. The Swiss fought with the halberd, an axe-blade and spike on a long shaft. From the 1420s they relied more on the pike, about 18 feet (5.5 m) long. Their dense squares could stand against horse and push other foot off the field.

Guns appear in European pictures and records from the 1320s. For a century they were noisy, slow and few. By the 1450s, though, the French royal artillery was knocking down English-held castles in Normandy in weeks.

Battles

Battles were rare, because one could lose a war in an afternoon. Most were short. They were decided by nerve, not by killing. When one side's line broke, its men ran, and the enemy cut them down from behind. Far more men died in the rout than in the fighting before it. The crusader graves at Sidon (1253) hold men cut down from behind, perhaps as they fled, and some perhaps beheaded after capture.

The English learned to fight on foot. Their men-at-arms dismounted and stood in line with the archers on their flanks or in front. They dug pits, set sharpened stakes, or chose ground behind a hedge or a slope. The enemy had to come to them through the arrows. The Portuguese and English at Aljubarrota fought the same way, behind a ditch and felled trees.

Sieges and raids

Most war was the taking and holding of strong places. A castle or walled town was besieged: blockaded, battered with stone-throwers, undermined, or stormed with ladders and towers. Many fell to hunger or a bargain, not an assault. A garrison that surrendered on terms usually walked out. One taken by storm could expect no mercy.

The other half of war was the raid. An English chevauchée burned and looted its way across France to ruin the enemy's lands and shame his king.

Women at the walls

On 25 June 1218 Simon de Montfort, leader of the crusade against the south, was besieging Toulouse. The townsmen sallied to burn his siege shelter, and he came up to drive them back. A stone from an engine on the walls struck him on the helmet and killed him. The Song of the Cathar Wars says the engine was worked by "ladies and girls and men's wives". A century later, in Scotland, Agnes, Countess of Dunbar, held Dunbar Castle against the Earl of Salisbury from January to June 1338 while her husband was away. Later Scottish tellings have her maids dusting the walls with cloths where the English stones had struck; that part is tradition.

Ransom and quarter

A knight was worth more alive. A captured man of rank could be held for ransom, often about a year's income or more, and the captor's lord took a share. King John II of France, taken at Poitiers in 1356, was ransomed for 3 million gold crowns. Common soldiers had less to offer and were more often killed. Quarter was a custom, not a right. Henry V had French prisoners killed at Agincourt when he feared a new attack. In 1499 the Swiss swore to take no prisoners at all.

Wounds

The mass graves at Visby (1361) and Towton (1461) show what the weapons did. At Visby most wounds were to the legs and the head, more on the left side than the right. At Towton most were to the head, and many skulls bear several blows.

A wounded man's chances depended on reaching help. Great lords had surgeons; the rank and file had barber-surgeons, or a comrade. They drew out arrows, stitched and bound wounds, and set bones. In 1403 John Bradmore drew an arrowhead from deep in the face of the young Prince Henry, cleaned the wound with wine and honey, and saved him. But no one knew what caused infection. Men who survived the field often died days later of fever and gangrene. A pierced belly or a deep wound to the chest was almost always fatal.

For the GM

Expect a medieval fight to be short and decided by nerve. Most men stop when they are hurt: the stop check and the side's morale roll end a skirmish within a minute or two. On the field map a melee takes ten or twenty minutes, and the side that breaks loses most of its men in the rout and the pursuit. Armour matters: it takes a wound down a step, a thrust beats mail better than a cut, and a war bow's arrows go through mail and a jack. Against plate, aim for a gap. A knight is worth taking alive. After the fight, wound fever kills many who lived through it; a camp and a good leech are the only help.

What is switched on

No module: the core rules are written for blades, bows and armour. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says, with no antibiotics and the camp's leech the only help.

Trouble at work

d10 Trouble
1 Hurt at the work: a fall, a kick or a blade. A light wound, and the rest of the term's pay is lost.
2 The employer won't pay, pays short or pays in clipped coin: half, unless he can be made to pay.
3 Taken before the justices for wages above the statute, or for vagrancy: fined a week's pay.
4 A brawl with rival workers, soldiers or locals: a Brawl check or a wound, and a grudge either way.
5 Fever, flux or plague in the lodging: a recovery check, or a week sick.
6 Robbed on the road or in bed: the term's earnings are gone.
7 Pressed into a lord's array or onto a king's ship, willing or not.
8 Falsely accused of theft or worse: find a witness, flee, or face the court.
9 Raiders, enemy soldiers or pirates fall on the place: a fight with a real enemy.
10 He saw something he should not have: a powerful man wants his silence, and may buy it or end it.

What each skill is for

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Ride Ride hard: Outride a pursuer, or catch a man who rides away. Ordinary the pursuer or the pursued (Ride) Away, or caught. Still close. Thrown: roll a fall as a wound.
Ride Swim a horse: Cross a deep ford or swim a river mounted. Hard — Across. Turned back. Swept away: Endurance check or drowned.
Seamanship Handle a boat: Take a boat across a river or along a coast; in rough water, hard. Ordinary — Across. Driven back. Swamped: Endurance check or drowned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Sidon, mid-13th century - crusader mass graves (bone evidence)

Bones of at least 25 men killed when Mamluk (1253) or Mongol (1260) forces sacked crusader Sidon, later gathered into the town ditch. Killed only.

How sure: taken directly from a source. From the study's table of bones with definite battle injuries (100 bones; 62 sharp, 35 blunt and 5 penetrating injuries) by body region. Sides are not recorded, and each region is shared among its locations by body exposure. Swords and axes roll on the sharp-force bones, the mace (spiked club) on the blunt-force ones and the spear on the penetrating ones (spiked mace, arrow, lance or javelin, the authors suggest); other weapons use all bones together.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Mikulski R.N.R., Schutkowski H., Smith M.J., Doumet-Serhal C. and Mitchell P.D., 'Weapon injuries in the crusader mass graves from a 13th century attack on the port city of Sidon (Lebanon)', PLoS ONE 16(8): e0256517 (2021), open access: S1 Table (elements with definite peri-mortem trauma by region).
  • Same study: more wounds on the back of the body than the front (men attacked as they fled); blows concentrated on the head, neck and shoulders, compatible with mounted attackers striking down at men on foot; one man had at least 12 injuries on 16 bones.
  • Tally: data/sources/sidon-1253-mass-graves.csv.

Sidon, mid-13th century - gameplay-adjusted (before armour)

Where blows land on a man fighting in the sack of a crusader town, before armour, re-weighted from the Sidon bone evidence without the neck cuts.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence.

Built from: Sidon, mid-13th century - crusader mass graves (bone evidence).

Rolled by: the battlefields of Jacob's Ford 1179, Sidon 1253; the armies of Latin East (c.1250), Ayyubids (c.1180).

Sources:

  • Derived from sidon-1253-mass-graves (Mikulski et al. 2021, S1 Table).

Visby 1361 - bone evidence

Melee, Gotland peasant levy (mail, shields, few helmets) vs Danish professional troops.

How sure: estimated to match published summary figures.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Thordeman, B. (ed.), Armour from the Battle of Wisby 1361, vol. I, 1939 - ch. IV, Ingelmark, B. E., 'The Skeletons', p. 149ff. (NOT YET READ - counts pending)
  • Summary figures: 1,185 individuals; 456 cut wounds; head wounds in 42.3% / 52.3% / 5.4% of graves 1-3 (Ingelmark, via Medievalists.net 2024).
  • Swedish History Museum: visible wounds concentrate on arms, legs and skulls; torso protected by mail and shields.

Visby 1361 - gameplay-adjusted

Same fight as the evidence table, re-weighted to where blows land before armour.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence.

Built from: Visby 1361 - bone evidence.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Visby 1361; the armies of Gotland and the Baltic (c.1360).

Sources:

  • Derived from visby-1361-evidence.

Aljubarrota 1385 - the São Jorge ossuary (bone evidence)

Leg bones of at least 414 men killed when the Portuguese and their English allies beat Castile and its French allies on 14 August 1385, gathered into an ossuary on the field. Killed only; long bones, few skulls.

How sure: taken directly from a source. From the 58 perimortem blunt-force fractures counted in 2,762 bone fragments (54 femur, 4 tibia; 41 left, 12 right, 5 side unknown). The side split is applied to both bones alike, an estimate: the paper's table of bone by side was not seen. The 52 sharp and puncture wounds of the earlier study (38 and 14, cuts on skulls, a crossbow bolt through a frontal bone, cuts on tibiae and femora) are not located by bone in what was published, and are left out.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Pérez Fernández Á., Alemán I., Botella M.C. and Cunha E., 'Perimortem fractures in the osteological collection of Aljubarrota (Portugal)', Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 40: 82-88 (2015), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0278416515000446 (summary): MNI 414 adults, all sexed fragments male, aged about 20-60; 58 blunt fractures, 72% in the middle third of the shaft, 69% on the front.
  • Cunha E. and Silva A.M., 'War lesions from the famous Portuguese medieval battle of Aljubarrota', International Journal of Osteoarchaeology 7(6): 595-599 (1997): cuts on crania (frontal and parietal), a frontal bone probably pierced by a crossbow bolt, cut marks on tibiae and femora, and many healed old injuries; no frequencies.
  • Tally: data/sources/aljubarrota-1385-ossuary.csv.

Towton 1461 - mass grave (bone evidence)

Death wounds on the men buried at Towton Hall after the battle of 29 March 1461, most likely Lancastrians caught in the rout. Killed only.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counted wound by wound from the study's tables: 124 head wounds (79 blade, 32 blunt, 13 penetrating) on 31 skulls and 56 injured bones below the head (52 blade, 4 blunt). Head wounds are counted per wound and body injuries per bone, as published, so the body is slightly under-counted. Blade weapons roll on the blade wounds, the poleaxe on the blunt ones and the dagger on the penetrating ones (arrow, bolt, dagger and poleaxe-spike wounds to the skull). Bows use all the wounds together. Unsided skull wounds (frontal, occipital, both parietals) are shared between left and right.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Holst M. and Sutherland T., 'Towton Revisited - Analysis of the Human Remains from the Battle of Towton 1461', in Eickhoff S. and Schopper F. (eds), Schlachtfeld und Massengrab: Spektren interdisziplinärer Auswertung von Orten der Gewalt (Zossen 2014), pp. 97-129: Tab. 9 (post-cranial injuries) and Tab. 12 (peri-mortem cranial weapon trauma).
  • Same chapter: 36% of the skeletons had peri-mortem injuries below the head (56 in all), mostly to the hands and forearms; the back of the skull, left parietal and left frontal took the most blade wounds. Its text gives 33 blunt (25%) and 13 penetrating (10%) head wounds; its table lists 124 head wounds, which this table follows.
  • Fiorato V., Boylston A. and Knüsel C. (eds), Blood Red Roses: the archaeology of a mass grave from the Battle of Towton AD 1461 (Oxbow, 2000; 2nd ed. 2007): the original excavation and analysis (Novak, 'Battle-related trauma').
  • Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/towton-1461-mass-grave.csv.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Crécy 1346, Aljubarrota 1385, Agincourt 1415, Towton 1461; the armies of England (c.1415-1460), France (c.1415), Portugal (c.1385), Castile (c.1385).

Dornach 1499 - the ossuary crania (bone evidence)

Skulls and thigh bones of men killed when the Swiss Confederates fell on the imperial camp below Dorneck on 22 July 1499, most of them the imperial dead, left out for a time and gathered into the ossuary. Killed only; skulls (no jaws) and femora.

How sure: taken directly from a source. From 417 perimortem injuries on 102 of 106 crania (315 cut, 69 point, 28 blunt, 5 gunshot) and 6 on 4 of 33 femora (Cooper 2010). Skull wounds are shared between the left and right of the skull by the author's sides for each kind (Table 28), midline ones evenly; the face's share is our tally from her catalogue. Swords and halberds (and the poleaxe) roll on the cuts, pikes and spears on the point wounds (thrust, stab and crossbow bolt counted together), the war hammer (spiked club) on the blunt ones, the handgun (and the matchlock) on the gunshot ones; others on all together.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Cooper C., Forensisch-anthropologische und traumatologische Untersuchungen an den menschlichen Skeletten aus der spätmittelalterlichen Schlacht von Dornach (1499 n. Chr.), Dr. phil. dissertation, Universität Mainz (2010), https://openscience.ub.uni-mainz.de/handle/20.500.12030/981 : Tables 23-32 and the lesion catalogue.
  • Cooper C., 'Kriegsverletzungen an historischen Skeletten aus der Schweiz', in Piek and Terberger (eds) (2008): a pilot of 12 skulls, 57 lesions.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Jacob's Ford, 30 August 1179 (the storm of the castle)

  • The armies: Templars and Ayyubids.
  • Fought for: the castle at Jacob's Ford, attacked by the Ayyubids.
  • The field: 40 by 70 hexes of 10 m, about 400 by 610 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the west, dusk.
  • Wounds: Sidon, mid-13th century - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Jacob's Ford, 1179 (Tiberias to Banias), at Chastellet (the castle at Jacob's Ford).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 121 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

In October 1178 King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem began a castle at Jacob's Ford on the upper Jordan. The ford was the crossing on the road from Tiberias towards Quneitra and Damascus. William of Tyre says the work took six months, and that the castle was a square with very thick walls. It was handed to the Templars, who already held Safed nearby.

Saladin saw the castle as a threat on his frontier. A lost Arabic source preserved by Abu Shama says he offered the Franks 60,000 dinars to pull it down, then raised the offer to 100,000. They refused. Taqi al-Din told him to spend the money on troops instead.

The spring and summer of 1179 went badly for the Franks. On 10 April Saladin's nephew Farrukh-Shah beat Baldwin's army near Banias, and the constable, Humphrey of Toron, was mortally wounded. On 10 June Saladin routed the Franks at Marj Ayyun and took the Templar master, Odo of St Amand, prisoner. In late August he came to the ford with his army. Baldwin gathered a relief force at Tiberias, about half a day's march to the south.

The places

  • Chastellet (the castle at Jacob's Ford): the Templar castle on a low rise west of the ford. Only its outer wall was finished. Excavation found one square tower at the south-west corner, a gate in the south wall and a postern on the east.
  • Jacob's Ford: the crossing of the Jordan between Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee. Arab writers called the place Bait al-Ahzan.
  • Tiberias: on the Sea of Galilee, where Baldwin assembled the relief army in August 1179.
  • Safed: a Templar castle in the hills to the west. Saladin's men cut timber in its district to shield their stone-throwers. Imad al-Din called it "a nest of evil".
  • Banias: the Ayyubid town north of the Hula. Near it, at Belfort, Farrukh-Shah beat Baldwin on 10 April 1179.
  • Hunin (Chastel Neuf): Humphrey of Toron's castle, where he died of his wounds in April 1179.
  • Quneitra: on the Golan, on the road from the ford to Damascus.

The leaders

  • Saladin (Ayyubid, sultan): commanded the siege in person and had the castle razed afterwards. His secretaries wrote the fullest accounts of it.
  • Farrukh-Shah (Ayyubid, Saladin's nephew): won the fight near Banias in April 1179 and later governed Damascus for his uncle. One Arabic account has him leading attacks on the castle from several sides.
  • Taqi al-Din (Ayyubid, adviser): urged Saladin to use the money offered for the castle on soldiers.
  • Al-Qadi al-Fadil (Ayyubid, Saladin's chief secretary): his letters give the garrison's strength, the wall's width and the commander's death.
  • Baldwin IV (Kingdom of Jerusalem, king): a teenager, already gravely ill. At Marj Ayyun he could not ride and a knight carried him to safety. His relief army arrived too late.
  • Odo of St Amand (Templars, master): oversaw the building. Captured at Marj Ayyun, he died in one of Saladin's prisons in 1180.
  • The castellan (Templars, commander): his name is not known. Al-Fadil says he threw himself into the fire as the castle fell.
  • Humphrey II of Toron (Kingdom of Jerusalem, constable): wounded near Banias in April 1179; he died soon after at Hunin.

The battle

Saladin arrived at the ford on a Saturday. His men took the outer compound on the first day. Ibn al-Athir credits a man in a torn tunic with climbing the wall first.

Saladin set up stone-throwers behind timber palisades. His archers shot at the walls from both sides; hundreds of arrowheads have been found on the east and west fronts. Meanwhile his miners dug under the north-east corner. Imad al-Din says the mine was 30 cubits deep, under a wall 9 cubits thick.

The miners propped the tunnel with timber and fired it, but the wall stood. Saladin then paid a dinar for every goatskin of water brought to put the fire out, so the sappers could go back in and dig deeper. News of the Frankish army at Tiberias hurried the work.

At daybreak on Thursday the second fire brought the corner down. Behind it the Franks had raised a timber wall; it caught fire in the wind, and the fire spread to their tents. The castle was stormed. Al-Fadil says the commander "threw himself into a hole full of fire". About 700 prisoners were taken. Imad al-Din says the volunteers killed most of them on the road. Saladin had the apostates and the bowmen put to death and sent the rest to Damascus.

That morning Baldwin set out from Tiberias. By noon his men saw the smoke, and he turned back. Al-Fadil counted about 1,000 mail shirts taken. The dead were thrown into the great cistern. In the heat a sickness broke out in Saladin's camp, and ten of his emirs died of it. Saladin stayed 14 days in all and had the castle pulled down.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The dates. Modern accounts give 23 or 24 August for Saladin's arrival and 29 or 30 August for the fall (Barber has the 24th and "Thursday, August 29th"). In the calendar of 1179, Saturday was 25 August and Thursday 30 August, which the game follows.
  • The garrison. Al-Fadil lists 80 knights with their squires and 15 captains with 50 men each, besides craftsmen and 100 Muslim slaves. Some modern summaries say 1,500 men.
  • The dead and the captured. Imad al-Din gives about 700 prisoners. Wikipedia gives both 800 killed and 700 taken, and the reverse. A 2011 press report spoke of 800 skeletons; the published study covers five, and the cistern has not been found.
  • The wall. Al-Fadil says it was over 10 cubits wide; Imad al-Din says 9 cubits thick. The excavators found it about 4 m thick, two faces of dressed stone round a core of basalt and lime, which fits the chroniclers. Ibn al-Athir calls the castle "impregnable", though it was unfinished and fell in under a week.
  • Who wanted the castle. Ernoul says the Templars persuaded Baldwin to break a promise not to build there. William of Tyre says the king began the work and gave it to the Templars.

Five men from the garrison

The Hebrew University's dig found five men of the garrison, aged 20 to 40, in the burnt ruin of a building that had fallen on them. One, numbered L.929, had his forehead split by a sword, his jaw cut through and his left arm severed at the elbow; three arrows had also struck his neck. A second had a sword cut into his left shoulder, a third an arrow in the pelvis. One showed no wound in the bone. Every sword wound was on the left side, as from right-handed men facing them, and none showed the neck cuts of an execution (Mitchell, Nagar and Ellenblum 2006).

Sources

  • Malcolm Barber, "Frontier warfare in the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem: the campaign of Jacob's Ford, 1178-79", in J. France and W. G. Zajac (eds), The Crusades and their Sources (1998), republished by De Re Militari: https://deremilitari.org/2013/12/frontier-warfare-in-the-latin-kingdom-of-jerusalem-the-campaign-of-jacobs-ford-1178-79/
  • Kate Raphael and others, The Excavation of the Templar Fortress at Jacob's Ford (1993-2009), Annual of the Nelson Glueck School of Biblical Archaeology XIII (2023): https://ngsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Templar_Fortress-Kate_Raphael-978-0-87820-511-0.pdf
  • Piers D. Mitchell, Yossi Nagar and Ronnie Ellenblum, "Weapon injuries in the 12th century Crusader garrison of Vadum Iacob Castle, Galilee", International Journal of Osteoarchaeology 16 (2) (2006): https://doi.org/10.1002/oa.814
  • "Jordan: Death and destruction at Jacob's Ford", Current World Archaeology 17 (2006): https://www.world-archaeology.com/features/jordan-death-and-destruction-at-jacobs-ford/
  • Wikipedia, "Siege of Jacob's Ford", "Battle of Marj Ayyun", "Odo of St Amand", "Farrukh Shah", "Daughters of Jacob Bridge" (consulted October 2026): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jacob%27s_Ford
  • "Remains of Crusader / Templar army discovered in Israel", Medievalists.net (2011): https://www.medievalists.net/2011/04/remains-of-crusader-templar-army-discovered-in-israel/

How the field is drawn

The storm of the castle at Jacob's Ford, 30 August 1179, at 10 m a hex: 40 x 70 hexes, about 400 m east to west and 600 m north to south, north at the top: the castle on the tell in the middle, its north-east corner fallen (rubble), the gate in the south wall, the postern on the east and the tower at the south-west; the Jordan down the east side and round the south, with the ford below the castle. The castle is drawn to the excavated figures, the tell, river and camp by hand; the walls are stone-wall edges (no crossing but the breach and the gates), the breach rubble. The garrison is al-Qadi al-Fadil's; Saladin's numbers are not known and the attackers are ours, with round numbers for play. The wounds roll on Sidon's table (the castle's own five skeletons are too few for one).

Sidon, 1253

  • The armies: Franks and Damascenes.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 110 by 90 hexes of 10 m, about 1,100 by 780 m, east at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Sidon, mid-13th century - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Sidon, 1253 (Banias to the coast), at Sidon.

The campaign

Louis IX of France invaded Egypt in 1249. In 1250 his army was beaten at Mansurah and he was taken prisoner on the retreat. Once ransomed, he did not go home. He stayed in the Holy Land until 1254 and spent much of his money on the walls of the crusader towns: Acre, Jaffa, Caesarea and Sidon.

Sidon was a port on the coast north of Tyre. The crusaders had built a castle on an islet off its harbour in 1227-1228, and another stood on a mound at the landward edge of the town. Louis's masons were rebuilding the town wall in 1253.

The Muslim powers were divided. Egypt was now ruled by the Mamluk Aybak, and Damascus by the Ayyubid an-Nasir Yusuf. Louis had bargained with Egypt against Damascus. In April 1253 the two made peace, with the caliph of Baghdad mediating. That left the army of Damascus free to strike at the Franks.

Later in 1253 that army came down on Sidon while the wall was still unfinished. Louis was not there.

The places

  • Sidon: the walled port, under repair in 1253, sacked that year and again in 1260.
  • Sea Castle: the crusader castle on its islet, about 80 m off the waterfront, built in 1227-1228 and completed under Louis IX.
  • Castle of St Louis (Qal'at al-Mu'izz): the land castle on its mound at the town's edge, built on the remains of an older fortress.
  • The town ditch: the ditch along the town's landward side. The two mass graves were dug into its floor, north-north-east of the land castle.
  • The gateway: a fortified gate in the town wall, with a crossing over the ditch, found close to the graves.
  • Acre: the chief city of the kingdom, whose walls Louis repaired first.
  • Jaffa: the southern port whose walls Louis also repaired.
  • Damascus: an-Nasir Yusuf's capital, inland beyond the mountains, from which the raid came.

The leaders

  • Louis IX (France, king): the crusade's leader. He paid for Sidon's walls and came afterwards to bury the dead.
  • Jean de Joinville (France, knight): Louis's companion, who wrote the eyewitness account of the king at Sidon.
  • An-Nasir Yusuf (Ayyubid, ruler of Damascus): his peace with Egypt in 1253 freed his army. In 1260 the Mongols took him prisoner and put him to death.
  • Aybak (Mamluk, sultan of Egypt): made peace with Damascus in April 1253 and was recognised as sultan.
  • Kitbuqa (Mongol, general): led the force that sacked Sidon in August 1260.
  • Julian Grenier (Franks, lord of Sidon): in 1260 he raided Damascene country and killed a Mongol officer, and the Mongols took their revenge on Sidon. He then sold the lordship to the Templars.

The battle

The written record is thin. L'Estoire d'Eracles says the attackers sacked the town, killed hundreds and took others prisoner. No account gives the hour, the strengths or the names of the captains.

The unfinished wall could not be held. The mass graves show what followed. The study by Mikulski and his colleagues counted at least 25 men and boys, from about 15 years old to elderly. There were no women or small children. Several had healed head wounds from earlier fights; some may have been soldiers.

Most of the dead had more wounds on the back than the front, so many were cut down as they ran. The blows fell mostly on the head, neck and shoulders. That fits horsemen striking down at men on foot. Some men had cuts on the hands and wrists, as if they had raised them against a blade. One man had at least 12 wounds on 16 bones.

Then there are the necks. Almost every man had a cut across the back of the neck. The authors think some captives were beheaded after the fight.

The bodies lay in the open for weeks before anyone buried them. They had been stripped; almost no weapons or valuables were found. Some bones were charred. When the dead were at last gathered, they went into a pit cut in the ditch floor, with more laid on the surface beside it.

Where the accounts disagree

  • 1253 or 1260. Sidon was sacked twice in seven years. A coin of Frederick II from about 1245-1250 and radiocarbon dates fit either. The authors favour 1253: the weeks of exposure match Joinville's account. Their abstract says only that the men "likely" died in one of the two attacks. The game dates the graves to 1253.
  • Who attacked. Mikulski and his colleagues, following Eracles, call the attackers "Mamluk forces from Damascus". In 1253 Damascus was ruled by the Ayyubid an-Nasir Yusuf, so many writers would call them Ayyubid. The game's wound table says Mamluk; its battlefield says an army from Damascus. Wikipedia's page on Sidon mentions an Ayyubid sack in 1249 and nothing in 1253.
  • Battle or execution. The neck wounds could be killing in the fight or beheading of prisoners after it. The authors lean towards executions for some.
  • Louis's burial. Joinville says the king buried the dead of 1253. Whether these are those same men cannot be proved.
  • The numbers. Eracles gives hundreds dead. No source gives either army's strength.

The king and the dead of Sidon

When Louis reached Sidon after the raid, the dead were still lying unburied. Joinville, who was with him, says the king "had personally carried the bodies, all rotting and stinking, to place them in trenches in the ground" (Caroline Smith's translation). Joinville adds that the king never covered his nose. Some 70 years later, an artist painting a prayer book for Queen Jeanne d'Évreux showed the scene among the deeds of Saint Louis. The graves dug at Sidon in 2015 held bodies exposed for weeks, as Joinville describes.

The wall, its unfinished stretch, the ditch, the gate and the ground are drawn by hand to the excavators' description, not traced from any map; the deployment is our own reading, in our own words, and the numbers are guesses for play.

Crécy, 26 August 1346 (the Vallée des Clercs)

  • The armies: English and French.
  • Fought for: the English position between Crécy and Wadicourt, attacked by the French.
  • The field: 200 by 160 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,390 m, west at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze from the west.
  • Wounds: Towton 1461 - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Crécy, 1346 (the Somme to Crécy), at the Vallée des Clercs (the battlefield).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 241 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Edward III of England claimed the French crown. In 1346 he landed at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy on 12 July, taking the French by surprise. His men stormed Caen on 26 July and looted it for five days.

The army marched east, burning as it went, and reached Poissy, about 20 miles from Paris. Philip VI of France shadowed it along the far bank of the Seine. On 16 August Edward turned north for the coast and the ships he expected at Le Crotoy. Philip reached the Somme first and held its bridges and fords.

On the morning of 24 August the English forced the tidal ford of Blanchetaque against Godemar du Fay. They plundered Noyelles and Le Crotoy for food, but no fleet was waiting. On 25 August they went round the Forest of Crécy and reached the slope above the Vallée des Clercs by evening, in Ponthieu, a county held by the English crown. Philip marched out from Abbeville on 26 August to find them.

The places

  • Abbeville: Philip VI's base and bridge on the Somme, which he left on 26 August.
  • Acheux-en-Vimeu: the English camp on the night before the ford.
  • Blanchetaque ford: a tidal ford across the Somme, passable a few hours twice a day; forced on 24 August.
  • Port-le-Grand: the north bank of the ford, where Godemar du Fay drew up about 3,500 men, 500 of them men-at-arms.
  • Noyelles-sur-Mer and Le Crotoy: towns north of the ford, looted for their stores and then burned.
  • Crécy: the town on the River Maye; the English right rested on it.
  • Wadicourt: the village at the northern end of the English line, anchoring its left.
  • The Vallée des Clercs: the valley below the English slope, where the French attacked; the accepted field since at least 1757.
  • Croix de Bohême: a stone cross where, by tradition, the blind King John of Bohemia fell.
  • Labroye (La Broye castle): where Philip came after dark on the night of the battle, asking to be let in.

The leaders

  • Edward III (English, king): 33 years old. He chose the ground and kept the third battle, his reserve, in his own hand.
  • Edward, Prince of Wales (English, first battle): later the Black Prince, then 16. His battle took the brunt of the charges.
  • William de Bohun, Earl of Northampton (English, constable): probably led the men-at-arms at Blanchetaque, and served with the Prince's battle, or with Arundel's, depending on the account.
  • Richard FitzAlan, Earl of Arundel (English, commander of the second battle).
  • Philip VI (French, king): had two horses killed under him and was hit in the jaw by an arrow.
  • John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia (French ally): blind, aged 50. He was killed with his escort.
  • Charles, Count of Alençon (French, Philip's brother): led the first men-at-arms through the Genoese, and was killed.
  • Antonio Doria and Carlo Grimaldi (French, captains of the Genoese crossbowmen): led the hired crossbowmen.
  • Godemar du Fay (French): held Blanchetaque and was routed.

The battle

French scouts found the English about noon on 26 August. Philip's council advised waiting a day, but the attack began about 17:00. Whether Philip chose this, or his front ranks pressed on, is not clear. The French unfurled the oriflamme, the banner that meant no prisoners.

The English stood on foot in three battles, their horses in a laager of carts behind, pits dug in front. Just before the fighting a thunder shower passed. The sun came out behind the English, in the French faces.

The Genoese crossbowmen went in first, tired from the march. Their pavises, the big shields they shot from behind, were still with the baggage. Froissart says the English archers shot "so thick that it seemed snow". The Genoese broke. The French men-at-arms behind them rode through them, cutting them down as they came.

Then came mounted charges up the slope, contingent after contingent as each arrived. They were disordered by the fleeing crossbowmen, the pits and the mud, and shot at from the flanks. The heaviest fighting fell on the Prince's battle. One report has the Prince beaten to his knees, his standard-bearer standing over the banner.

The sun set about 18:40 and the charges went on into the dark. Philip's own battle went in late, and the oriflamme was left on the field. About midnight Philip left the field with a handful of men. At La Broye he called at the gate: "Open your gate quickly, for this is the fortune of France" (Froissart, Berners' translation). By morning he was at Amiens.

The English slept on the field. Next morning, in mist, mounted English men-at-arms caught French levies still coming up and cut them up. On 4 September Edward laid siege to Calais. It fell on 3 August 1347.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The English army. Ayton puts it at about 14,000 and Rogers at 15,000. Sumption, working from what the fleet could carry, gives 7,000-10,000.
  • The French army. Chroniclers give 72,000 or 120,000. Modern estimates are about 8,000 mounted men-at-arms, 2,000-6,000 crossbowmen and an unknown number of foot. Schnerb doubts the higher crossbow figure.
  • The losses. The heralds counted 1,542 French knights and squires dead, not counting the next day's. Froissart's heralds give 1,200 knights "and more than thirty thousand other". An English roll-call found about 40 dead; some historians suggest 300.
  • The number of charges. Knighton counts 16 attacks before dawn; later writers often say 15. Rogers and Ayton doubt any fixed number.
  • The oriflamme. Sumption has it left on the field; DeVries has it captured when its bearer fell; yet Miles de Noyers, who carried it, lived until 1350.
  • The Prince's danger. Froissart has Edward refuse him help, saying to "suffer him this day to win his spurs". Other accounts have the King send men from the reserve.
  • The site. The Vallée des Clercs has been accepted since at least 1757, but no archaeology of a large battle has been found there. Michael Livingston (2015) argues the fight was by the Forest of Crécy, about 5.5 km south.

One stroke with my sword

John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia, was blind. He rode with Philip as an ally. When he heard how the battle was going, he asked where his son was. Then he called on his knights to lead him forward, so "that I may strike one stroke with my sword" (Froissart, Berners' translation). So that they would not lose him in the press, his companions tied the reins of their bridles to each other and put the King in front. They rode into the English line in the failing light. All of them were killed.

How the field is drawn

The battle of Crécy, 26 August 1346, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 160 hexes, about 2000 m south to north and 1390 m west to east, west at the top: the wood and the wagon park behind, the English on the ridge and its slope from Crécy and the Maye (left) towards Wadicourt (right), the windmill behind the middle; the Vallée des Clercs across the middle, its far side a steep bank open only at its ends; the Estrées plateau below it, and the way in from the Fontaine-sur-Maye road at bottom left. The ridge, the valley, the bank and the terraces are drawn to the accounts' words (Preston's bank; the terraces from an unsourced guide), not traced from any survey. The bank plays as an earth bank (slow to cross, high side the plateau's): the rules have no edge horses cannot cross, so it only slows them. The pits play as stakes. The English guns (ribalds under the carts) are not on the field. The strengths are Froissart's battles for the English and Sumption's figures for the French, split among the bodies the chroniclers name, with round numbers for play; most of the French foot never came up. Men-at-arms on both sides wear the coat of plates and mail of the 1340s.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The Genoese come on About 17:00, as the shower passes: the crossbowmen, tired, without their pavises and their strings wet, come up the valley with three shouts; the archers step forward and shoot 'so thick that it seemed snow'.
16 Alençon rides through them The Genoese break; the Count of Alençon's men ride them down and on at the Prince's battle (when is our reading).
31 The King of Bohemia The blind king is led in, his knights' reins tied to his; all are killed.
61 The charges go on Lorraine, Blois and Flanders come up, contingent by contingent (Knighton counts sixteen charges in all; Blois dismounted his men for the last).
101 Sunset 18:40: the sun goes down behind the English.
121 Philip's battle The King's own battle and what foot had come up go in; two horses are killed under Philip and an arrow strikes his face (when is our reading).

Visby, 27 July 1361

  • The armies: Gotlanders and Danes.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 80 by 70 hexes of 10 m, about 800 by 610 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Visby 1361 - gameplay-adjusted.
  • On the travel map: Gotland, 1361 (the landing to Visby), at Visby.

The campaign

Valdemar IV of Denmark, called Atterdag, took Scania back from Magnus Eriksson of Sweden in 1360. Gotland was the next prize. The island was Swedish in name but ran its own affairs, and Visby was a rich Hanseatic town on the Baltic trade routes. Town and countryside did not get on.

Magnus warned Visby by letter on 1 May 1361 that an attack was coming. Valdemar's fleet sailed first to Öland, where his men took the tower at Borgholm. On 22 July about 30 ships, some of them cogs, were seen off Stora Karlsö. The army landed on Gotland's west coast that day, perhaps 2,000 to 2,500 men, many of them hired Germans.

The Gotland farmers called out their district levies. They tried to stop the Danes at Ajmunds bridge on the road to Visby, and were beaten on 24 July at Fjäle mire beside it. The Danes reached Visby on 26 July, ahead of the levies. The townsmen shut their gates.

The places

  • Vivesholm: near Klintehamn; one of the two likely landing places.
  • Kronvald: a fishing place on the Eksta coast; the other likely landing place.
  • Ajmunds bridge: near Mästerby, on the fastest road to Visby across the Sudertingsån; the levies chose to hold it.
  • Fjäle mire: about 1 km east of the bridge, where the bog narrows to about 150 m. It was dry enough to cross that summer, and the levies were beaten there on 24 July.
  • Visby: the walled Hanseatic town. Its gates stayed shut during the battle, and it let Valdemar in on 29 July.
  • Söderport: the south gate of the ring wall, outside which the battle was fought.
  • Solberga nunnery: the Cistercian house outside the wall; the dead were buried by its cemetery.
  • Korsbetningen: "the Cross Meadow", the town's pasture outside the wall, named from the memorial cross over the graves. The graves were dug up in 1905, 1912 and 1928-1930, the last by Bengt Thordeman, who published Armour from the Battle of Wisby in 1939.

The leaders

  • Valdemar IV Atterdag (Danish, king): about 40 years old. He led the invasion and afterwards added "King of Gotland" to his titles.
  • Christopher, Duke of Lolland (Danish, the king's son): about 20. He rode into Visby beside his father on 29 July.
  • Eric of Lauenburg (Danish ally): a north German lord named among Valdemar's commanders.
  • The Gotland commanders (Gotlanders): their names are lost. The levy was organised in six divisions.
  • Magnus Eriksson (Swedish, king): Gotland's overlord. He warned Visby of the attack by letter in May.

The battle

No account gives the hour or the order of the fight in any detail. What follows comes from the chronicles, modern reconstructions and the bones.

On 27 July the levies came up to Visby and found the Danes between them and the wall. The Danish crossbowmen shot first. One modern account believes they knocked out about a fifth of the levy before the lines met. The graves bear this out: Ingelmark counted 126 arrow and bolt wounds, and some men had been hit five, six or seven times. The shafts seem to have come from every side.

Then came the hand-to-hand fight, and the farmers lost it. Many were boys, old men or men with old injuries, in old-fashioned kit. Against them stood professionals in mail and plate. A Lübeck chronicle put the defeat down to the farmers being unarmed and unused to war. The town kept its gates shut.

Ingelmark recorded 456 wounds from swords and axes. Most were to the legs; a mail coat and a shield kept most blows off the body. One man lost both lower legs, probably to a single stroke. One skull has 15 cuts and holes. Some men were cut down from behind, struck on the back of the head as they ran. Some leg wounds were probably given after a man was already down.

About 1,800 Gotlanders died, by the Franciscan chronicle of Visby. Danish losses are unknown; one modern figure is about 300.

The dead lay in the July heat. They were thrown into pits by Solberga's cemetery, many still in their mail, mail hoods and coats of plates; it was too hot, and there were too many, to strip them. On 29 July Valdemar and Christopher rode into Visby. That day the king issued a charter confirming the town's old rights and freedoms. A copy made in 1425 survives.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. Modern accounts give the Danes 2,000-2,500 men and the Gotland levy about 5,000 in all. Neither rests on a count made at the time.
  • The dead. The Franciscan chronicle gives 1,800 Gotlanders. The bones recovered number 1,185 (Ingelmark). The Swedish History Museum lists 256, 798 and 119 skeletons from the first three graves, with a fourth grave left mostly undug. A popular account puts the first grave at 300.
  • The third grave. Some of its men lay in rows, east to west, with little armour: wounded men who died later, or Danes given a proper burial (the museum offers both).
  • The surrender. One story, still told as fact in some summaries, has Valdemar break through the wall. Others have the council open the gates after two days. The charter of 29 July fits a bargain better than a storm.
  • The plunder. The Franciscan chronicle says Valdemar took home "a priceless treasure of gold and silver" from town and country; the Zealand Chronicle adds furs. A Visby letter of 1362 says the Hanse's goods were saved by a payment. The museum finds no evidence that the town was sacked.

Three barrels of silver (a legend)

Visby's best-known story is a legend. In it, Valdemar has three great beer barrels set up in the square. The town must fill them with gold and silver by a set time, or he will burn it. The burghers fill them, and the king sails off with his loot. No source written at the time records the barrels. The chronicles speak only of treasure taken, and the town was taxed rather than burned. One chronicle does say a Danish ship, laden with goods from the churches and the townsmen, was wrecked off the Karlsö islands on the way home. Carl Gustaf Hellqvist painted the scene in Munich in 1882, with a dachshund, a breed of the 16th century, in the crowd.

Aljubarrota, 14 August 1385 (the plateau of São Jorge)

  • The armies: Portuguese and Castilians.
  • Fought for: the Portuguese position at São Jorge, attacked by the Castilians.
  • The field: 100 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Towton 1461 - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Aljubarrota, 1385 (Leiria to Alcobaça), at São Jorge (the battlefield).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 61 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Fernando I of Portugal died in October 1383 without a son. By treaty his crown would pass to his daughter Beatriz, wife of Juan I of Castile. Lisbon would not have it, and made João, Master of Avis, Fernando's half-brother, defender of the realm. Juan besieged Lisbon in 1384 and failed. In March and April 1385 the Cortes of Coimbra made João king.

Juan invaded again in July 1385, with French lances and the Portuguese nobles who held for Beatriz. He came down by Coimbra to Leiria. João and his Constable, Nuno Álvares Pereira, gathered at Tomar, marched by Ourém and camped at Porto de Mós on 12-13 August, across the road to Lisbon. Some 640 English soldiers, landed at Easter, were with them.

On the morning of 14 August the Portuguese drew up on the plateau of São Jorge, facing north towards Leiria. About noon the head of the Castilian column came up, saw them across the road, and would not attack there.

The places

  • Leiria: the Castilian base on 12-14 August.
  • Ourém: the Portuguese marched through it on 11 August.
  • Porto de Mós: the Portuguese camp on 12-13 August.
  • The first position: where the Portuguese drew up on the morning of the 14th, facing Leiria, about 2 km north of the field.
  • Calvaria de Cima: the village the Castilians passed as they went round the Portuguese to the west.
  • Chão da Feira: the open ground south of the field where the Castilians halted and formed up.
  • São Jorge: the plateau between two stream valleys where the battle was fought. The chapel of São Jorge, built by Nuno Álvares in 1393, stands about where his vanguard stood.
  • Aljubarrota: the village the battle is named after, 11 km away.
  • Alcobaça: the Cistercian abbey where the Portuguese went on 17 August.
  • Santarém: where Juan I fled on the night of the battle.

The leaders

  • João I (Portuguese, king): king since April. He led the rearguard.
  • Nuno Álvares Pereira (Portuguese, Constable): 25 years old, winner at Atoleiros in 1384. He chose the ground and led the vanguard.
  • Mem Rodrigues and Rui Mendes de Vasconcelos (Portuguese, the wing of young knights later called the Ala dos Namorados): Lopes puts it on the right; Mem Rodrigues was wounded.
  • Antão Vasques de Almada (Portuguese, the other wing, with the foreigners).
  • Gonzalo Núñez de Guzmán, Master of Alcántara (Castilian, a wing): took the light horse round to the Portuguese rear.
  • Guillaume de Montferrant (Portuguese side, Gascon knight): joined the army at Tomar in August and was killed in the battle.
  • Juan I (Castilian, king): claimed Portugal through his wife. He was ill and had been carried in a litter for some two weeks (Ayala).
  • Pedro Álvares Pereira (Castilian, Master of Calatrava): Nuno's elder brother, who had gone over to Castile. He was killed.
  • João Afonso Telo, Count of Barcelos (Castilian side): brother of the dowager queen Leonor Teles. He was killed, the only enemy dead whom João I had buried.
  • Jean de Rye (French, a leader of the French contingent): killed with many of his men.
  • Pero López de Ayala (Castilian, chancellor): fought, was taken prisoner, and later wrote the Castilian account of the battle.

The battle

The Castilians went round the Portuguese to the west, by Calvaria, and halted on the open ground of Chão da Feira, to the south. In the early afternoon the Portuguese turned about. They moved about 2 km south and formed up facing south, on a narrow front between the two valleys. In front of them they dug a ditch and rows of pits.

By Ayala's account, charges of cowardice pushed the Castilian council to attack. About 18:00 the Castilian bombards fired first; one shot killed two squires, brothers, in the Portuguese vanguard (Lopes). Then the vanguard, mostly French, with the Portuguese loyalists, came on. It met the pits and the ditch, and was shot at from the wings by the English archers and the Portuguese crossbowmen. The Castilian crossbowmen and foot had been left behind.

The vanguards met on the narrow front. The Portuguese killed the French knights they had taken prisoner, so as not to have them at their backs (by the Portuguese chronicles and Froissart). Then Juan's main battle came up behind its vanguard. The valleys funnelled it in, and it could not use its numbers. Many of its men had dismounted to fight on foot.

Near sunset the Castilian royal standard fell, and the army broke. The Master of Alcántara's light horse got round to the Portuguese rear and the baggage, where crossbowmen and foot beat them off (Lopes, Ayala). The fighting had lasted under an hour. The Portuguese followed while the light lasted.

Juan rode about 50 km that night to Santarém, then went by boat down the Tagus to his fleet and on to Seville. Thousands more Castilians were killed in the next day or two by the country people around Leiria. Castile went into mourning. The Portuguese held the field the customary three days, then marched to Alcobaça on 17 August. João vowed an abbey for the victory, at Batalha, begun in 1386.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. Fernão Lopes gives the Portuguese 1,700 lances, 800 crossbowmen and 4,000 foot. Older estimates give Castile about 31,000. Monteiro (2001) puts it nearer 20,000, and argues (2006) that the Castilians did not outnumber the Portuguese in the fighting itself.
  • The English. Lopes counts only 200 foreigners. Froissart gives 200 in one version and 500 in another. The Westminster chronicler gives about 700. Russell (1962), from the English records, has about 640, some 300 of them archers.
  • The field works. Froissart, Juan I's own letter of 29 August 1385 and the Crónica del Despensero say the Portuguese fortified the field. Ayala, who was there, says nothing of it. Lopes writes as if there were none. The digs of 1958-1960 found a large ditch and some 830 pits.
  • The "square". Later tradition has Nuno form his men in a hollow square. Monteiro argues it never existed: the valleys and the works did the job.
  • The first charge. Some accounts have the French charge on horseback; others have them come on foot, or dismount under fire.
  • The attack on the rear. Lopes and Ayala give it to the Master of Alcántara's light horse; some modern accounts give it to Pedro Álvares Pereira, Master of Calatrava.
  • The wings. Lopes puts the Ala dos Namorados on the right; many modern accounts put it on the left. The name "Ala da Madressilva" for the other wing is later tradition.
  • The losses. Modern figures are about 4,000 Castilians killed on the field and about 5,000 more in the rout, against about 1,000 Portuguese. The ossuary on the field holds about 2,800 bones from more than 400 men.

The English at Aljubarrota

On Easter Sunday, 2 April 1385, two ships reached Lisbon with 200 men-at-arms, 200 archers and 400 moios of wheat. A third ship landed 90 men at Setúbal, and a fourth about 150 at Porto. They had been mustered at Plymouth and paid three months in advance from 24 March. The muster orders name captains such as Peter Cressingham, Robert Grantham and Thomas Dale. Fernão Lopes, writing some 50 years later, made little of them. Peter Russell found their muster orders in the Public Record Office in London, and argued that their 300 or so bows, beside Lopes's 800 crossbows, gave João more firepower than the chronicle admits.

How the field is drawn

The battle of Aljubarrota on the plateau of São Jorge, 14 August 1385, at 10 m a hex: 100 x 130 hexes, about 1000 m east to west and 1130 m north to south, north at the top: the Portuguese facing south about the chapel's ground, with the ditches in front and the pit field on their right; a stream valley on each side; the Castilians coming up from Chão da Feira at the bottom. The valleys, the ditches and the pit field are drawn to the excavated and chronicle figures, not traced from any plan; the pits play as stakes. The strengths are Fernão Lopes's, split among the bodies he names, with round numbers for play; the Castilian crossbowmen and foot, left behind by the King, are not on the field, nor the bombards, which fired once to little effect. The wounds roll on Towton's table; the ossuary's bone evidence is its own table.

The phases

From exchange Phase What happens
1 The bombards and the advance About 18:00: the Castilian trons fire (one shot kills two squires, brothers) and the French and loyalist vanguard comes on into the pits and the shot from the wings.
16 The vanguards meet In the gap between the valleys; the Castilian wings cannot come up level with their vanguard. Prisoners taken in the first clash are killed.

Agincourt, 25 October 1415

  • The armies: English and French.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 100 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Towton 1461 - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Agincourt campaign, 1415 (Harfleur to Calais), at Azincourt.

The campaign

Henry V reopened the war with France in 1415, while the French princes were divided between the Armagnac and Burgundian factions. He landed at Chef-en-Caux in the Seine estuary on 13 August with about 9,000 men. On 18 August his army closed round Harfleur. Raoul de Gaucourt held the town until 22 September.

The siege cost Henry dearly in sickness. Anne Curry's count of the sick lists finds 1,330 men sent home ill. The Earl of Suffolk died there. Henry left a garrison of 300 men-at-arms and 900 archers in Harfleur.

On 8 October he set out for Calais by the coast road through Fécamp, Arques and Eu. On 13 October he found the Blanchetaque ford held against him. The army turned up the Somme looking for a way over, with the French vanguard under d'Albret and Boucicaut keeping pace on the far bank. Food ran short. On 19 October the English crossed by the causeways at Béthencourt and Voyennes. They marched north, crossed the Ternoise on 24 October and found the French across their road near Azincourt.

The places

  • Harfleur: the port at the Seine mouth, besieged from 18 August and taken on 22 September.
  • Blanchetaque ford: Edward III's crossing of the Somme in 1346; found held on 13 October.
  • Péronne: the town on the Somme just north of where the English crossed.
  • Béthencourt ford and Voyennes ford: the crossings the English used on 19 October; the causeway at Voyennes was undefended.
  • Blangy: where the army crossed the Ternoise on 24 October.
  • Azincourt: the village at the west side of the field, which gave the battle its name.
  • Tramecourt: the village and woods at the other side of the field. The ground between narrowed towards the English.
  • Calais: English since 1347, the march's goal.

The leaders

  • Henry V (English, king): 29. He took the main battle in the centre and fought on foot.
  • Edward, Duke of York (English, the vaward on the right): he had led the van on the march. He was killed in the press.
  • Thomas, Lord Camoys (English, the rearward on the left).
  • Sir Thomas Erpingham (English, the archers): about 60, an old soldier of Henry IV's. He gave the signal to advance.
  • Charles d'Albret (French, Constable of France): an Armagnac and joint commander in name. He led the vanguard and was killed.
  • Jean le Maingre, called Boucicaut (French, Marshal of France): a veteran of Nicopolis (1396). He was captured and died a prisoner in Yorkshire in 1421.
  • The Dukes of Alençon and Bar (French, the main battle): both were killed.
  • Charles, Duke of Orléans (French, with the vanguard): captured and taken to England.
  • Ysembart d'Azincourt (French): led a small band of men-at-arms and some 600 peasants against the English baggage.

The battle

The armies sighted each other on the evening of 24 October. Both spent the night in the open, in heavy rain. Henry ordered silence in his camp. In the morning the French stood between the woods across his road. Their men-at-arms stood on foot in a vanguard and a main battle, with mounted wings to ride down the archers and a rearguard of mounted servants. The ground between was freshly ploughed and soaked.

For about three hours after sunrise neither side moved. The French could wait; the hungry English could not. Erpingham threw up his baton and called out a word the French chroniclers wrote as "Nestrocq". The English went forward to long bowshot, about 250-300 m, pulled up their stakes and planted them again, and began to shoot. The musée de l'Armée puts this about 11:00.

The French mounted wings, under strength, charged. A few riders, among them Guillaume de Saveuse, reached the stakes and were killed. The rest turned, and wounded horses bolted back through their own vanguard.

The vanguard then came on through the mud. Under the arrows the French crowded in towards the English men-at-arms, the narrowing ground squeezing them closer. Men fell and could not rise; some were crushed or smothered. When their arrows ran out the archers left the stakes and fell on the French flanks with swords, hatchets and the mallets they had used to drive the stakes. York died in this fighting. Henry stood over his wounded brother Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, and took an axe blow on his helmet. The main battle came on behind the vanguard and fared no better; Alençon was killed in it.

Late in the fight word came that the English baggage was being plundered. At the same time the Counts of Marle and Fauquembergues gathered about 600 horsemen for a fresh attack. Henry, with many prisoners still armed behind his line, ordered them killed, sparing only the greatest. The counter-attack failed and both counts died. The rest of the French rearguard went away.

The order to kill the prisoners

The English men-at-arms would not do it. Killing men who had surrendered was beneath them, and each prisoner was a ransom lost. So Henry gave the work to a squire with 200 archers. Jean le Fèvre, who was with the English army, saw the prisoners "cut in pieces, heads and faces". Men whose helmets were off were easy; others were stabbed through the eye-slits of their bascinets. When the last French attack broke, Henry stopped the killing. Hundreds of prisoners survived, and most chroniclers of the time blamed the French lords who forced his hand rather than Henry.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. Curry, from the pay records, gives about 9,000 English (8,500 in another count) against about 12,000 French. Rogers, Barker and Sumption put the English at about 6,000. Sumption gives the French about 14,000; Rogers about 24,000, counting the armed servants; Barker at least four to one.
  • The French losses. The heralds counted 3,069 knights and squires dead, with at least 2,600 more bodies unidentified, about 6,000 in all. Prisoners are put at 700 to 2,200.
  • The English losses. The records name at least 112 dead. Monstrelet gives 600; Wavrin 1,600.
  • The length of the fight. Most accounts give about 3 hours. The musée de l'Armée has the fighting go on until about 17:00.
  • The baggage raid. Barker, following the Gesta Henrici Quinti, puts it at the start; others put it late, as a trigger for the killing.
  • The site. The traditional field lies between the Tramecourt woods and Azincourt. Metal-detector surveys there have found no trace of the battle. Michael Livingston has argued for ground west of Azincourt.

Towton, 29 March 1461

  • The armies: Yorkists and Lancastrians.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Snow, strong wind from the south.
  • Wounds: Towton 1461 - gameplay-adjusted (before armour).
  • On the travel map: Towton campaign, 1461 (Pontefract to York), at Towton.

The campaign

Richard, Duke of York, claimed the throne of Henry VI. The Act of Accord of 1460 made him Henry's heir, but Queen Margaret would not see her son disinherited. Her army killed York near Wakefield on 30 December 1460. It then beat Warwick at St Albans and took back the King. London shut its gates, and the army fell back to York.

York's son Edward, Earl of March, joined Warwick in London. He was proclaimed king on 4 March 1461 and marched north after the Lancastrians in three bodies: Lord Fauconberg leading, Edward with the main army, and the Duke of Norfolk raising men in the east to follow on.

The Yorkists gathered round Pontefract on 27 and 28 March. Henry VI and Margaret waited at York. Their army, under the Duke of Somerset, lay at Tadcaster across the road.

The places

  • Pontefract: where the Yorkist army gathered before the battle.
  • Ferrybridge: the Aire crossing, its bridge broken by the Lancastrians. Warwick's men forced it on 27 March and were surprised there next dawn.
  • Castleford ford: a ford upstream, where Fauconberg crossed to get behind Clifford.
  • Dintingdale: a valley about a mile south of the Lancastrian line, where Clifford was caught and killed.
  • Saxton: the village just behind the Yorkist line.
  • Towton: the village behind the Lancastrian line, about 2 miles south of Tadcaster.
  • Towton Dale: a shallow valley across the plateau. The Lancastrians drew up on its north side.
  • Castle Hill Wood: woodland on the western edge, where Waurin says Lancastrian horsemen hid.
  • Cock Beck: a steep-sided stream, in flood, west of the plateau. Many fleeing Lancastrians died crossing it, by what is still called Bloody Meadow.
  • Tadcaster: the Wharfe crossing on the road to York, where the rout made for.
  • York: where Henry VI and Margaret waited.

The leaders

  • Edward IV (York, king): 18 years old. He fought on foot and steadied his left wing when it gave way.
  • William Neville, Lord Fauconberg (York, vanward): Warwick's uncle. He crossed at Castleford and led the archers. He was made Earl of Kent.
  • Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick (York): hit in the leg by an arrow at Ferrybridge.
  • John Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk (York): raised men in the east. His contingent came up the old London road late in the day and turned the battle.
  • Henry Beaufort, Duke of Somerset (Lancaster, commander): the victor of Wakefield and St Albans. He chose to stand and let the Yorkists come to him. He escaped to Scotland.
  • Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland (Lancaster): late to guard the Castleford ford on 28 March. He was killed in the battle.
  • Sir Andrew Trollope (Lancaster): a professional soldier, much respected. He was killed.
  • John, Lord Clifford (Lancaster): led the dawn attack at Ferrybridge. He was killed at Dintingdale by an arrow in the throat.

The battle

Before dawn on 28 March Lord Clifford and John, Lord Neville fell on the Yorkists camped at Ferrybridge. Lord Fitzwalter was mortally wounded rallying his men. Warwick's half-brother, the Bastard of Salisbury, was killed. Edward fought for the narrow crossing while Fauconberg crossed upstream at Castleford. Clifford fell back and was caught and killed at Dintingdale.

On Palm Sunday, 29 March, the armies drew up on the plateau between Saxton and Towton, the Lancastrians on the north side of Towton Dale. Hall says the fighting began about 09:00. Snow began as the lines formed. The wind blew it from the south into the Lancastrians' faces. Norfolk had not yet come.

Fauconberg's archers shot at long range, then stepped back. The Lancastrian archers replied into the wind and snow. Their arrows fell short. When they had shot all they had, the Yorkists came forward, gathered the spent arrows from the ground and shot them back.

The Lancastrians had to attack. Waurin says horsemen hidden in Castle Hill Wood broke the Yorkist left, and that Edward himself steadied it. The lines then fought hand to hand for hours, the Lancastrians feeding in fresh men. The Yorkists were pushed slowly back up the southern ridge.

Norfolk's men came up the old London road unseen and fell on the Lancastrian left. The Lancastrian line broke. Men threw off their armour to run. Both sides had ordered no quarter. Many were cut down from behind or after they gave up.

The worst of the killing was at Cock Beck. The chronicles say the dead lay so thick in the water that men crossed on them. The chase went on to the Wharfe at Tadcaster, where a bridge gave way and more drowned. Henry VI and Margaret fled from York to Scotland. Edward was crowned that June.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The numbers. Gregory's Chronicle claims hundreds of thousands. Historic England gives about 80,000 on the field, most modern writers 50,000-65,000. The Battlefields Trust doubts either side had more than about 10,000.
  • The dead. The heralds counted 28,000, and Hall 36,776. Ross and Wolffe preferred the Annales rerum anglicarum's 9,000 Lancastrians. Tim Sutherland suggests 2,800-3,800, with Ferrybridge and Dintingdale counted in.
  • One day or two. No contemporary source names 28 March; they say "Palm Sunday eve". Sutherland argues Ferrybridge, Dintingdale and Towton were one running fight starting before dawn on the 29th.
  • How long. Hall says about nine hours, Polydore Vergil ten. George Neville's letter has the fighting from dawn until the tenth hour of night. English Heritage estimates about three hours.
  • The story itself. The snow, the arrows and Norfolk come from Hall, writing about 70 years later. Waurin, the only detailed 15th-century account, has none of them, nor Cock Beck; he alone has the Castle Hill Wood ambush.

Towton 16

In 1996 builders putting up a garage at Towton Hall found a grave of about 38 men from the battle. Most had died of blows to the head, many from behind; Shannon Novak counted earlier, healed wounds on nine of 28 skulls. One man, numbered Towton 16, was about 45-50 years old. Long before 1461 a blade had cut deep into the left side of his lower jaw and broken it. It had healed well, leaving a rounded scar in the bone below his first molar (Knüsel, 2005). He still went to Towton. Caroline Wilkinson and Richard Neave rebuilt his face from the skull in 2003, scar and all.
